stem: A child has swallowed a non-battery foreign body that has passed through the oesophagus; what is the best counselling statement?

options.text: Once an object has passed through the oesophagus, it is most likely to pass PR via the digestive tract
Any object beyond the oesophagus routinely needs theatre removal
Once it passes the oesophagus, it usually lodges in the palatine tonsils
Passage beyond the oesophagus predicts right-sided lung hyperinflation
CT is always required once the object enters the stomach

explanation: Once an object has passed through the oesophagus, it is most likely to pass PR via the digestive tract. In this situation, reassurance is usually appropriate for a non-battery foreign body because most such objects continue through the gut, although button batteries are an important exception.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf p.142

optionExplanations.A: Correct because once a swallowed non-battery foreign body has passed through the oesophagus, it is most likely to pass PR via the digestive tract.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because objects beyond the oesophagus do not routinely require theatre removal and many will pass spontaneously.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because palatine tonsils are not the expected site for an object that has already passed the oesophagus.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because right-sided lung hyperinflation is associated with aspiration, not a swallowed foreign body passing through the oesophagus.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because CT is not always required once the object enters the stomach; management is usually guided by the object type and symptoms.

sourceRefs: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
